_readme: All player-facing chrome that isn't level data. Edit here, not in index.html.
{handSlots} and {rowLen} are filled in at render time from the current run,
so the help screen can never disagree with the game again.
title: Tidy Adventures
tagline: Everything Everywhere All in its place
_jobBoardNote: The campaign screen: one tile per level, in play order, showing the face of
whoever hired you. Clients come from data/clients.json; these are the words
the board itself uses. `sub` takes {done} and {total}. `lockedTile` is the
name on a client you haven't met — keep it short, it sits under a face in a
tile about 80px wide, and keep it anonymous: the silhouette is the joke.
_titleScreenNote: The Continue card. It is the same component as the win screen's next-job
card (see winScreen below) with different copy: that one pitches a job you
have not started, this one names the person you left standing in a half-tidy
house. {room} is the room the save was in and {left} is how many items are
still out — both read straight off the parsed save, which is never loaded
THIS CARD IS THE ONE THAT QUOTES THE CLIENT. It shows the stage `teaser` —
the ask, still outstanding — and the win screen's card deliberately does
not, even though it is the same component. The teasers were written from
the same beats as the intros, so quoting one in front of a job that has NOT
started prints the client's opening line before they get to say it. Here
the job is underway and the intro has been heard, so the same line is a
NO ARTICLE GOES NEAR {room}. Room names supply their own and they disagree:
"Kitchen" and "Attic" want "the", "The Familiar's Roost" already has one,
and "Hydroponics" wants none. "You left off in the {room}" produced "in the
the Familiar's Roost" and "in the Hydroponics" on the same build. The room
is named in the card's FOOTER instead, where it is a label rather than part
of a sentence, and the body line talks about the floor.

titleScreen.leftOff: Still {left} things on the floor in there.
titleScreen.leftOffClear: The floor is clear — go and finish it.

_winScreenNote: The card at the top of the win screen. The COPY on it is per-stage (`hook`
in clients.json); these are only the labels around it, so a rename never
ONE LINE ONLY, AND IT IS THE HOOK. A hook is the client making contact —
how they got hold of you, what working for you once has changed — which is
the right thing to put in front of a job that has not started. The stage
`teaser` used to sit under it and it was a spoiler: the teasers were
authored from the same beats as the intros, so the card printed the
client's opening line before the client said it (3-2's teaser is "ok that
was ONE party. one." and its intro opens "ok before you say anything: that
was one party"). The teaser still renders on the Continue card, where the
intro has already been heard — see _titleScreenNote.
_jobSizeNote: HOW BIG IS THIS JOB, in words. The campaign fluctuates job size against the
client's own story arc — a first job is a look-in, a second is the real
work, a third is everything they have — and a player who cannot see that
just feels that some levels took longer. The band is DERIVED from the
level's own numbers (rooms x cont x types x rowLen, in js/data.js), never
authored, so it cannot disagree with the job it is describing.
Ordered smallest first. "upTo" is the largest item count in the band; the
LAST entry must omit it and is the catch-all. Boot validation checks both.
"pip" is the compact form for a job-board tile, which has room for about
three characters beside the id — keep it to marks, not words. Small squares
were the first try and all but vanished at 9px on a phone; a filled circle
is the smallest mark that still reads as one at that size.
Retune these and the labels move; retune the levels and the labels follow.
The one thing not to do is write a size onto a level.
For reference: outside the tutorial the smallest job is about 90 items and
the biggest about 700, every client's arc climbs across its stages, and no
two jobs in a row are within a fifth of each other. Boot validation warns
if either of those last two stops being true.
_freePlayNote: THE FREE PLAY BOARD. Size bands from data/sizes.json crossed with the cast
from data/clients.json, five houses each. These are the words the board
itself uses; the place names on the tiles are `places` on each client and
the band names are `label` on each band.
`sub` takes {done} and {total} — the whole board. `bandSub` takes {done}
and {total} for one band and {who} for how many characters are in it, which
is what stops a short row reading as a missing tile: The Dream is a
four-room world and honestly cannot offer a 1,800-item house, so it is not
listed under the big bands at all (see `reach` in sizes.json).
`tileItems` takes {n}, already thousands-separated. It is the count the run
will ACTUALLY hold, derived per world, never the band's authored target.

freePlay.title: Free Play
freePlay.allDone: Every house on the board. All of them.

jobBoard.title: Job Board
jobBoard.sub: Who needs you today. {done} of {total} done.

_houseVoiceNote: FREE PLAY HAS NO CLIENT, and these are the lines the house uses instead.
Same six situations as `quips` in clients.json (door, cache, unlock, room,
misfile, nothing) plus `nudge` for coming back to a half-tidied house.
The voice is the same hand that signs a free-play note — the one "— M"
belongs to. Fond, faintly amused, and never chatty: a client has a stake in
the job and can afford a joke, whereas the house is only keeping you
company. Keep these SHORTER than a client's for that reason.
These are also the fallback for a campaign client missing a quip, so every
situation must be covered here even if every client covers it too. `face` is
the emoji the bubble wears when nobody was hired; a themed free-play run
prefers the theme's own `icon` from themes.json and only falls back to this.
{room} {container} {item} are filled in; the same token rules as quips.

cache: Coins, in a box, in a house nobody lives in. Fine.
unlock: {container} gives up whatever it was holding onto.
room: Nothing left on the floor in {room}.
nothing: None of that lives in this room.
nudge: You left this one half done. It has waited.

helpIntro: Everything's on the floor. Every item belongs in one specific piece of furniture — the fridge, the toolbox, the shoe rack. Toss things in, then open them up and sort the rows. A row of {rowLen} matching items glows gold; finish every row in every container.

helpBullets.b: Pinch, scroll or double-tap the floor
helpBullets.text: — zoom in and out (drag to look around)
— it files itself into the right row
— look inside; drag items out to toss them on the floor
— tap a hand slot to file that item

helpBullets.b: Drag out of a hand slot
helpBullets.text: — put it down anywhere on the floor
— toss it back on the floor
— what's inside; gold aura = that set is done; red = it doesn't live there
— some doors and furniture need keys; drag keys onto the lock
— cross a threshold and you pick a new talent
